mean: steady and clear in what you say; not easily changed by pressure
ex: Ritu stayed polite but firm until the Lajpat Nagar shopkeeper agreed to refund the faulty mixer.
note: Firm is not rude. You can be warm in tone and still firm on the point.
ex2: The coach gave the parents a firm answer: only players who attend practice will go to the district trials.

mean: to say clearly that you will not do or accept something
ex: Anil decided to refuse the extra weekend shift because he had promised his daughter a trip to the Hyderabad zoo.
note: Refuse + to-verb: 'I refuse to sign.' Not 'I refused for signing'.
ex2: Senior nurses at the district hospital refuse to skip the hand-washing rule, however busy the ward gets.

mean: making people follow rules exactly, with no exceptions
ex: Our hostel warden in Shillong was strict about the ten o'clock gate, even on festival nights.
note: Strict is about rules; firm is about your own position. A parent can be firm without being strict about everything.
ex2: The umpire was strict about the time limit for reviews, and the captain missed his chance by two seconds.

mean: to ask for something strongly, as your right
ex: Passengers on the delayed Rajdhani had every right to demand hot food and a clear update from the staff.
note: As a verb, no 'for': 'demand an apology', not 'demand for an apology'. At work, 'request' is softer.
ex2: The tenants met on Sunday to demand that the landlord fix the leaking water tank before the monsoon.

mean: to give up your position because someone pushes you
ex: When the builder raised the price again, Fatima did not back down and showed him the signed agreement.
note: Changing your mind because of good evidence is wise. Backing down only because of pressure is the problem.
ex2: Neither captain would back down over the disputed catch, so the gully match went to the third umpire: Nani on her balcony.

mean: a limit you set on what others may ask of you or do to you
ex: Kavya set a clear boundary with her team: no work calls after 9 p.m. unless a server is down.
note: In cricket a boundary is a four or a six; in life it is a line you protect. Setting one is not selfish.
ex2: Ramesh told his relatives kindly that his salary is a boundary he will not discuss at family weddings.

mean: to disagree with or resist a plan or request
ex: If the client wants the app in two weeks, push back and explain what a rushed launch will break.
note: It also means 'postpone': 'push back the meeting to Friday'. The context tells you which.
ex2: Teachers at the Kochi school decided to push back on the plan for extra tests every Saturday.

mean: to keep your position even when people pressure you
ex: If the recruiter says the offer is final, hold your ground politely and ask again about the joining bonus.
note: Change 'your' to fit: 'she held her ground'. Holding your ground is calm, not loud.
ex2: 'Hold your ground!' the coach shouted as the bigger boys charged at the young defenders on the Kolkata maidan.

mean: fixed; not open to discussion or change
ex: For Dr Iyer, a seatbelt for every child in the car is non-negotiable, even for a five-minute drive.
note: Use it sparingly. If everything is non-negotiable, nothing is, and people stop taking you seriously.
ex2: At our small Jaipur startup, honesty with customers is non-negotiable, even when the truth costs us a sale.

mean: to use your authority to stop something firmly
ex: If the kids are on their phones at dinner every night, put your foot down and make it a no-screen meal.
note: Change 'your' to fit: 'Dad put his foot down.' It suggests authority, so it sounds odd when used towards your boss.
ex2: As a new manager, you may need to put your foot down when meetings keep starting forty minutes late.

mean: having decided firmly to do something and not letting anything stop you
ex: Determined to clear the exam, Sana studied in the railway waiting room whenever the power went off in her village.
note: Say 'determined to do', not 'determined for doing'.
ex2: The determined fielder chased the ball all the way to the rope and saved four runs in the last over.

mean: firm and clear about a decision, even when it is hard
ex: The sarpanch stayed resolute about the tree-planting plan, though some families wanted the land for parking.
note: Resolute is admiring: firm for a good reason. If the firmness is unreasonable, say stubborn.
ex2: Even after two failed startups, Joseph was resolute that his third idea, cheap cold storage for farmers, would work.

mean: staying steady and strong; never becoming weaker or doubtful
ex: Her husband's unwavering support helped Lakshmi through three years of night classes for her law degree.
note: Usually goes with support, faith, focus or commitment. It is about steadiness, not volume.
ex2: The goalkeeper's unwavering focus during the penalty shootout won Odisha the hockey title.

mean: to accept that a task, decision or mistake is yours to handle
ex: Instead of blaming the vendor, Priya chose to take ownership of the delayed launch and fixed the plan herself.
note: Owning a decision is part of being firm: 'I decided this, and I will answer for it.'
ex2: Good captains take ownership of a loss at the press conference instead of blaming the pitch.

mean: refusing to lower your standards or accept less
ex: The old tailor in Chandni Chowk is uncompromising about fit and will redo a sherwani three times.
note: Can be praise (high standards) or criticism (never meets anyone halfway). Your tone decides which.
ex2: Our English teacher's uncompromising red pen made our Class 10 essays shorter, sharper and far better.

mean: to set a limit on what you will accept
ex: Jokes among old friends are fine, but I draw the line at mocking someone's accent.
with: know where to draw the line
note: Pattern: 'draw the line at + noun or -ing': 'I draw the line at lying.'
ex2: The housing society lets residents decorate freely for every festival, but had to draw the line at loudspeakers after 10 p.m.

mean: calm and in control of your feelings, especially under pressure
ex: When an angry customer shouted at the Bengaluru branch, Teresa stayed composed and explained the bank's rule clearly.
note: Being composed gives quiet authority: people listen more to a calm 'no' than to a loud one.
ex2: The young batter looked composed at the crease, needing twelve off the last over in front of a packed Chepauk.

mean: loyal and firm for a long time, without changing
ex: Through the long court case over the family land, Baljit remained steadfast and never signed the false papers.
note: Steadfast suggests loyalty over time, to a person, a value or a cause.
ex2: Her steadfast friend Ayesha visited the hospital every evening for a month after the accident.

mean: refusing to change your mind, however much people argue
ex: Dadi was adamant that the wedding lunch would be served on banana leaves, caterer or no caterer.
note: Stronger than firm, and it can hint at stubbornness. Use 'adamant that...' or 'adamant about...'.
ex2: The founder was adamant that no customer data would be sold, whatever the investors said.

mean: not showing fear or doubt, even when facing something hard
ex: The junior engineer gave an unflinching account of the bridge's weak points to the safety committee.
note: To flinch is to pull back quickly from pain. Unflinching honesty means telling hard truths calmly.
ex2: The documentary takes an unflinching look at the water crisis in Chennai's outer suburbs.

mean: a serious, calm manner that makes people respect you
ex: The new principal spoke softly, but she had such gravitas that the noisy assembly went silent.
note: Gravitas comes from calm and substance, not from a loud voice or big words.
ex2: The veteran news anchor's gravitas made even a short weather update sound important.

mean: not saying sorry for something you believe is right
ex: Meenakshi was unapologetic about leaving the office at six to pick up her son from school.
note: Healthy about a fair choice; arrogant about a real mistake. Know which one you are defending.
ex2: The chef at the Lucknow dhaba is unapologetic about his biryani taking forty minutes: good food needs time.

mean: refusing to change your view or agree, even when it is unreasonable
ex: Talks over the canal water broke down because both villages stayed intransigent about the timing.
note: This is firmness gone too far. Learn it to know the line: firm people listen, intransigent people do not.
ex2: The landlord was so intransigent about the deposit that the tenants finally took the matter to court.

mean: staying completely calm, even when things go wrong
ex: The imperturbable station master calmly guided thousands off the platform when the Mumbai local broke down.
note: A rare, formal word. In speech, 'unflappable' is more common and means the same.
ex2: Our imperturbable chemistry teacher didn't even blink when the experiment filled the lab with smoke.
